BRUSSELS — When EU foreign ministers left their Monday session without a signed 21st sanctions package, the failure landed on the same day the bloc's revised Russian oil-price cap was meant to take hold. The two deadlines were supposed to reinforce each other. The oil cap arrived on schedule; the enforcement meant to sit beside it did not.

## Brussels Blinks at the Oil-Cap Deadline

The text ministers carried into the room had already been softened to court reluctant capitals — a concession made before the bargaining even began. ## The Night the Lights Went Out in Balaklava

Part of Sevastopol went dark overnight into 14 July, and the Kerch Bridge closed while the strikes were underway. Those are the facts almost no one disputes.

The rest came from Mikhail Razvozhaev, the Moscow-installed governor, who narrated the night in stages. First: air defenses and mobile fire groups had thrown gunfire into the dark over the Balaklava district, on the southern edge of the city, and brought down five drones, with no one hurt. Then the fuller version — the drones had reached energy infrastructure, part of the city had lost power, and a special regime was now in force at the affected facilities while specialists tallied the damage and emergency crews stood at full readiness. Conserve your phone battery, he told residents; use your devices only for emergencies, and don't overload the network.

Ukrainian reporting sharpened the outline his account left blurred. The monitoring channel "Krymsky Viter" logged explosions and gunfire in Kerch, where occupation authorities had shut the bridge, and named the targets its watchers could only infer — the Balaklava thermal power station and a 110-kilovolt substation, "Shiroke," out in the Baidar Valley. Blasts were heard near Cape Fiolent and Sapun Hill. Carried by focus.ua, the reporting tied the night to the wider campaign against Crimean infrastructure and to earlier remarks by drone commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi. No Ukrainian military source claimed the strike.

Widen the frame and the single night dissolves into a longer siege. Bulgaria's fakti.bg cast Sevastopol as a city in slow collapse — halted public transport, business curfews, darkened streets, schooling gone remote — and reached for the Institute for the Study of War's phrase about a "new phase of full maritime isolation of Crimea." It put a number on the strain: more than 4.3 billion rubles, roughly 56 million dollars, allocated by Moscow to cover shuttered businesses and a wrecked tourist season.

## Windows in a Boarding School, Cars Ablaze in Darnytskyi: Kyiv's Fourth Ballistic Night in a Week

The crater opened in the ground beside a boarding school. Its blast pushed out windows in the main building and the annex, though the walls held and no child was hurt. Not far off, in the Darnytskyi district, debris dropped into an open lot and set several parked cars alight. In Holosiivskyi, warehouses burned until emergency crews put the fires down. This was Kyiv at roughly 00:15 on July 14, when the air-raid sirens began, some twenty minutes before the explosions came.

The threat had been tracked from the Bryansk area: around six to eight modified ballistic missiles, described in several accounts as adapted S-400s, aimed at the capital. Mayor Vitali Klitschko, Kyiv Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko, and the State Emergency Service each reported the same outcome — damage across at least four addresses, courtyards littered with debris, and no dead or wounded in the city. The figures wobble at the edges: Warsaw's niezalezna.pl, citing open-source trackers, put the count at eight and claimed roughly half were intercepted, while Ukrainian outlets dwelt on the shortage of Patriot interceptors rather than any tally of missiles brought down.

Moscow described the same night in entirely different terms. The Russian Defence Ministry said its long-range precision weapons and drones had struck military-industrial plants producing missiles and drones in Kyiv, along with fuel-storage infrastructure at Port Yuzhny in the Odesa region, and a tanker en route from Chornomorsk. Where Ukrainian accounts counted broken windows, burning cars, and a scorched schoolyard, the Russian one counted only weapons factories and fuel depots — a night reduced to a target list.

The strike sat inside a wider, near-continuous exchange. Ukrainian drones drew air-defence fire and shut down the Moscow-area airports of Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky, with interceptions reported over Belgorod, Kursk and Bryansk — a strand fakti.bg of Bulgaria pushed to the center while others let it slip to the margins. Elsewhere, separate Russian drone strikes wounded 11 people in Zaporizhzhia and six near Kharkiv. And it all landed only hours after Ukraine, France and other European states gathered in Paris to announce "Freya," a nine-plus-nation coalition to build European anti-ballistic defenses, a project Volodymyr Zelensky called historic against the backdrop of a Patriot shortfall he has not stopped naming.

By now the sequence is familiar — ballistic alerts over Kyiv on July 8, July 11, and again here — the reason this reads less as a single event than as the standing weather of the war.

## A Sanctions Bill Becomes Lindsey Graham's Epitaph

What hangs in the balance after Lindsey Graham's death is not a memorial resolution but a piece of legislation with real teeth: a bipartisan bill that would let the US president impose secondary sanctions and tariffs on any country still buying Russian oil, uranium, and natural gas. Two days before he died, Graham stood in Kyiv and announced he had secured a White House agreement to advance exactly that measure. His death has now converted a long-stalled bill into a test of whether the Senate will pass it as a tribute to the man who spent his final weeks pushing it.

Graham, 71, the South Carolina Republican who had held his seat since 2002 and chaired the Senate Budget Committee, died late Saturday of a ruptured aorta brought on by atherosclerotic heart disease. On Friday he had met President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv, appearing alongside Senators Richard Blumenthal, Jeanne Shaheen, and Roger Wicker to unveil the revised sanctions package. Within a day of his death, Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Senator Chuck Grassley were calling on Congress to enact the bill in his honour, and CNN's reporting that the White House would back the bipartisan version supplied the political mechanism to make that possible. No Trump administration statement in its own words has surfaced; the endorsement reaches the reader secondhand.

How much his absence costs Ukraine is where the coverage pulls apart. To American and Ukrainian eyes, the loss is strategic. A Washington Post analysis casts Graham as the rare figure who could "speak Trump's language," golf outings and all, and warns that his removal could stall both the sanctions bill and a NATO Patriot co-production licensing deal while leaving pro-Ukraine Republicans exposed; Ukraine's ambassador in Washington, Olga Stefanishina, makes the same case. Russian commentators start from the opposite premise. Dmitry Evstafyev of the HSE reads Trump's support as an almost foregone symbolic gesture — no faction in Congress objects to squeezing Moscow, and the bill hands the president discretionary authority he could just as easily turn on Russia or, Evstafyev suggests, on Ukraine. MGIMO's Alexei Zudin is blunter still: Graham's death, he says, "will not fully close the path to sanctions." A channel to Trump severed, or a legislative process that grinds on with or without any single senator — the choice of frame decides the stakes.

The two records do not even agree on who Graham was. In Moscow's telling he was an entry on Rosfinmonitoring's registry of "terrorists and extremists." That detail never surfaces in the Ukrainian, Bulgarian, or Lithuanian coverage, which remembered a senator who, by Zelensky's count, had come to Ukraine ten times since the full-scale invasion and stayed at work on sanctions and air-defence initiatives to the last.

Whether the bill now moves is the immediate question. The votes Thune and Grassley are calling for would give the president a discretionary lever over every major buyer of Russian energy — and turn a bill that languished for months into the fastest-moving item on the Senate's Ukraine agenda, carried by the death of the man who wrote it.

Graham, 71, der Republikaner aus South Carolina, der seinen Sitz seit 2002 hielt und den Haushaltsausschuss des Senats leitete, starb am späten Samstag an einer Aortenruptur infolge einer atherosklerotischen Herzerkrankung. Russische Kommentatoren gehen von der entgegengesetzten Prämisse aus. Dmitri Jewstafjew von der HSE liest Trumps Unterstützung als nahezu ausgemachte symbolische Geste — keine Fraktion im Kongress habe etwas dagegen, Moskau in die Zange zu nehmen, und das Gesetz gebe dem Präsidenten einen Ermessensspielraum, den er ebenso gut gegen Russland wie, so deutet Jewstafjew an, gegen die Ukraine wenden könnte. Alexei Sudin vom MGIMO ist noch schroffer: Grahams Tod, sagt er, „wird den Weg zu Sanktionen nicht vollständig verschließen". Ob sich das Gesetz jetzt bewegt, ist die unmittelbare Frage. Die Abstimmungen, die Thune und Grassley fordern, gäben dem Präsidenten einen Ermessenshebel gegenüber jedem großen Abnehmer russischer Energie — und machten aus einem Entwurf, der monatelang dahindümpelte, das am schnellsten laufende Vorhaben auf der Ukraine-Agenda des Senats, getragen vom Tod des Mannes, der ihn schrieb.

После смерти Линдси Грэма на весах висит не мемориальная резолюция, а закон с настоящими зубами: двухпартийный законопроект, который позволил бы президенту США вводить вторичные санкции и пошлины против любой страны, всё ещё покупающей российские нефть, уран и природный газ. Грэм, 71 год, республиканец от Южной Каролины, удерживавший своё кресло с 2002 года и возглавлявший бюджетный комитет Сената, умер поздно вечером в субботу от разрыва аорты, вызванного атеросклеротической болезнью сердца. ## A Sanctions Bill Becomes Lindsey Graham's Epitaph

What hangs in the balance after Lindsey Graham's death is not a memorial resolution but a piece of legislation with real teeth: a bipartisan bill that would let the US president impose secondary sanctions and tariffs on any country still buying Russian oil, uranium, and natural gas. Two days before he died, Graham stood in Kyiv and announced he had secured a White House agreement to advance exactly that measure. His death has now converted a long-stalled bill into a test of whether the Senate will pass it as a tribute to the man who spent his final weeks pushing it.

Graham, 71, the South Carolina Republican who had held his seat since 2002 and chaired the Senate Budget Committee, died late Saturday of a ruptured aorta brought on by atherosclerotic heart disease. On Friday he had met President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv, appearing alongside Senators Richard Blumenthal, Jeanne Shaheen, and Roger Wicker to unveil the revised sanctions package. Within a day of his death, Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Senator Chuck Grassley were calling on Congress to enact the bill in his honour, and CNN's reporting that the White House would back the bipartisan version supplied the political mechanism to make that possible. No Trump administration statement in its own words has surfaced; the endorsement reaches the reader secondhand.

How much his absence costs Ukraine is where the coverage pulls apart. To American and Ukrainian eyes, the loss is strategic. A Washington Post analysis casts Graham as the rare figure who could "speak Trump's language," golf outings and all, and warns that his removal could stall both the sanctions bill and a NATO Patriot co-production licensing deal while leaving pro-Ukraine Republicans exposed; Ukraine's ambassador in Washington, Olga Stefanishina, makes the same case. Russian commentators start from the opposite premise. Dmitry Evstafyev of the HSE reads Trump's support as an almost foregone symbolic gesture — no faction in Congress objects to squeezing Moscow, and the bill hands the president discretionary authority he could just as easily turn on Russia or, Evstafyev suggests, on Ukraine. MGIMO's Alexei Zudin is blunter still: Graham's death, he says, "will not fully close the path to sanctions." A channel to Trump severed, or a legislative process that grinds on with or without any single senator — the choice of frame decides the stakes.

The two records do not even agree on who Graham was. In Moscow's telling he was an entry on Rosfinmonitoring's registry of "terrorists and extremists." That detail never surfaces in the Ukrainian, Bulgarian, or Lithuanian coverage, which remembered a senator who, by Zelensky's count, had come to Ukraine ten times since the full-scale invasion and stayed at work on sanctions and air-defence initiatives to the last.

Whether the bill now moves is the immediate question. title: Fifty Minutes Over Kyiv: One Strike, Two Official Records

## Fifty Minutes Over Kyiv: One Strike, Two Official Records

By mid-morning on 14 July, two official accounts of the same night stood on file, and they did not describe the same city.

The Russian Ministry of Defence, in its daily statement, reported strikes by long-range precision air- and ground-launched weapons and drones on military-industrial enterprises producing missiles and drones in Kyiv, and on fuel-and-lubricant port infrastructure at Yuzhny, Odesa oblast. The statement listed targets. It listed no addresses, no fires, no casualties. Russian agencies carried it in that form, placing the night in a series of precision strikes on ports and defense plants: Chornomorsk, Odesa, Izmail, now Yuzhny.

Kyiv's municipal record, filed hours earlier by Mayor Klitschko, military administrator Tkachenko and the DSNS emergency service, listed addresses. Warehouse and storage buildings burning at two sites in Holosiivskyi district. Cars alight on open ground in Darnytskyi. A crater beside a boarding school, its windows blown out. Debris in residential yards. No dead, no injured in the capital — a detail present in every Ukrainian account and absent from every Russian one.

The two records share almost nothing but the hour.

The sequence, unspooled: air-raid alarms sounded in the capital shortly after midnight, around 00:15. Explosions followed within minutes — at least six by Ukrainian counts, six to eight in Bulgarian and Croatian accounts. Poland's Niezalezna put the attack at eight modified S-400 ballistic missiles, roughly four of them intercepted — a figure that sits awkwardly beside the Ukrainian side's own emphasis, where the operative fact is an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors and, per 24tv, a night three days earlier when none of six Iskander-M missiles were downed. Even the car fires in Darnytskyi carry two explanations: falling debris from an intercepted weapon, per Klitschko; direct impact, implied elsewhere. The alert lifted after roughly fifty minutes.

The night was wider than Kyiv, and each record trims a different edge of it. Drones injured eleven people in Zaporizhzhia and six near Kharkiv — casualties that appear nowhere in the Russian statement. Meanwhile Ukrainian drones flew over Moscow, airports closed, and strikes were reported at Sevastopol and a Donetsk ammunition depot — traffic that the Kyiv record leaves out, and that Bulgarian and Serbian outlets, working from both sides' statements, restored. Fakti.bg filed the night as symmetrical escalation over two capitals. Russia's ura.news went further, organizing its account around Ukrainian strikes said to have damaged warehouses and gas stations in Ukraine's own south — the Kyiv strike displaced from its own story.

Unspool one step further back and the timing acquires its frame. Hours before the alarms, in Paris, nine European states — Britain, France, Germany and the Nordics among them — announced an anti-ballistic coalition, designated "Freyja" and described as purely defensive. President Zelensky called it historic and set his requirement at roughly 100 Patriot missiles per month. Much of the Central and Eastern European press built its accounts on that juxtaposition: a ballistic strike on the capital, hours after Europe pledged a ballistic shield, against a capital short of interceptors. The same timing could be run in the opposite key — Greece's Bankingnews amplified President Putin's warning that Ukrainian strikes would be answered "with multiplied force," and set the night within reports of Russian ground advances.

By late morning, the accounts had sorted themselves into three currents. Ukrainian outlets converged on the boarding school and the interception gap, with RFE/RL's Ukrainian service extending toward a war-crimes framing. Russian outlets converged on the target list and the logic of a series. A third group — Serbia's Politika, Bulgaria's Fakti — held both records side by side without ruling. What no account produced, from any direction, was an answer to the central question: whether what burned in Holosiivskyi was a missile plant or a warehouse. Each side's designation hardened rather than moved.

That is the displacement this fourth ballistic night in a week leaves on the record. The munitions counts differ by two; the interception claims differ by four; but those are details. The structural gap is between an account organized around targets and an account organized around addresses — and after fifty minutes of alert and a full day of statements, no source stands between them with an independent inspection of either site. The next round of Patriot deliveries, which Zelensky says he expects within days, will be measured against whichever record a reader has accepted — a shield judged by one ledger, a failure by the other.

# Fünfzig Minuten über Kiew: ein Schlag, zwei amtliche Protokolle

Bis zum Vormittag des 14. Juli lagen zwei amtliche Darstellungen derselben Nacht zu den Akten — und sie beschrieben nicht dieselbe Stadt.

Das russische Verteidigungsministerium meldete in seiner täglichen Erklärung Schläge mit weitreichenden Präzisionswaffen luft- und bodengestützter Art sowie Drohnen gegen militärisch-industrielle Betriebe, die in Kiew Raketen und Drohnen produzieren, und gegen die Hafeninfrastruktur für Treib- und Schmierstoffe in Juschny, Oblast Odesa. Die Erklärung listete Ziele auf. Sie listete keine Adressen, keine Brände, keine Opfer. Die russischen Agenturen übernahmen sie in dieser Form und stellten die Nacht in eine Serie von Präzisionsschlägen gegen Häfen und Rüstungswerke: Tschornomorsk, Odesa, Ismajil, nun Juschny.

Das städtische Protokoll Kiews, Stunden zuvor eingereicht von Bürgermeister Klitschko, Militärverwalter Tkatschenko und dem Katastrophenschutz DSNS, listete Adressen auf. Lager- und Speichergebäude, die an zwei Stellen im Bezirk Holosijiwskyj brannten. Autos in Flammen auf offenem Gelände in Darnyzkyj. Ein Krater neben einem Internat, dessen Fenster herausgesprengt waren. Trümmer in Wohnhöfen. Keine Toten, keine Verletzten in der Hauptstadt — ein Detail, das in jeder ukrainischen Darstellung vorkommt und in jeder russischen fehlt.

Die beiden Protokolle teilen fast nichts außer der Uhrzeit.

Die Abfolge, abgespult: Kurz nach Mitternacht, gegen 00:15 Uhr, heulten in der Hauptstadt die Luftalarmsirenen. Die Explosionen folgten binnen Minuten — mindestens sechs nach ukrainischer Zählung, sechs bis acht in bulgarischen und kroatischen Berichten. Polens Niezalezna bezifferte den Angriff auf acht modifizierte ballistische S-400-Raketen, davon rund vier abgefangen — eine Zahl, die sperrig neben der eigenen Betonung der ukrainischen Seite steht, wo der operative Fakt ein akuter Mangel an Patriot-Abfangraketen ist und, laut 24tv, eine Nacht drei Tage zuvor, in der keine von sechs Iskander-M-Raketen heruntergeholt wurde. Selbst die Autobrände in Darnyzkyj tragen zwei Erklärungen: herabfallende Trümmer einer abgefangenen Waffe, so Klitschko; direkter Einschlag, andernorts nahegelegt. Nach rund fünfzig Minuten wurde der Alarm aufgehoben.

Die Nacht war größer als Kiew, und jedes Protokoll beschneidet eine andere Kante von ihr. Drohnen verletzten elf Menschen in Saporischschja und sechs bei Charkiw — Opfer, die in der russischen Erklärung nirgends auftauchen. Unterdessen flogen ukrainische Drohnen über Moskau, Flughäfen schlossen, und Schläge wurden aus Sewastopol und von einem Munitionsdepot in Donezk gemeldet — Verkehr, den das Kiewer Protokoll auslässt und den bulgarische und serbische Medien, die aus den Erklärungen beider Seiten arbeiteten, wiederherstellten. Fakti.bg verbuchte die Nacht als symmetrische Eskalation über zwei Hauptstädten. Russlands ura.news ging weiter und organisierte seine Darstellung um ukrainische Schläge, die Lagerhäuser und Tankstellen im eigenen Süden der Ukraine beschädigt haben sollen — der Schlag auf Kiew, aus seiner eigenen Geschichte verdrängt.

Spult man einen Schritt weiter zurück, bekommt das Timing seinen Rahmen. Stunden vor den Alarmen kündigten in Paris neun europäische Staaten — darunter Großbritannien, Frankreich, Deutschland und die Nordländer — eine Anti-Ballistik-Koalition an, „Freyja" getauft und als rein defensiv beschrieben. Präsident Selenskyj nannte sie historisch und bezifferte seinen Bedarf auf rund 100 Patriot-Raketen pro Monat. Ein Großteil der mittel- und osteuropäischen Presse baute seine Berichte auf dieser Gegenüberstellung auf: ein ballistischer Schlag auf die Hauptstadt, Stunden nachdem Europa einen ballistischen Schild versprochen hatte, gegen eine Hauptstadt, der die Abfangraketen ausgehen. Dasselbe Timing ließ sich auch in der Gegentonart spielen — Griechenlands Bankingnews verstärkte Präsident Putins Warnung, ukrainische Schläge würden „mit vervielfachter Kraft" beantwortet, und stellte die Nacht in Berichte über russische Geländegewinne.

Bis zum späten Vormittag hatten sich die Darstellungen in drei Strömungen sortiert. Ukrainische Medien liefen beim Internat und der Abfanglücke zusammen, wobei der ukrainische Dienst von RFE/RL sich in Richtung einer Kriegsverbrechens-Rahmung streckte. Russische Medien liefen bei der Zielliste und der Logik einer Serie zusammen. Eine dritte Gruppe — Serbiens Politika, Bulgariens Fakti — hielt beide Protokolle nebeneinander, ohne zu richten. Was keine Darstellung lieferte, aus keiner Richtung, war eine Antwort auf die zentrale Frage: ob das, was in Holosijiwskyj brannte, ein Raketenwerk war oder ein Lagerhaus. Die Zuschreibung jeder Seite verhärtete sich, statt sich zu bewegen.

The statement listed targets. It listed no addresses, no fires, no casualties. Russian agencies carried it in that form, placing the night in a series of precision strikes on ports and defense plants: Chornomorsk, Odesa, Izmail, now Yuzhny.

Kyiv's municipal record, filed hours earlier by Mayor Klitschko, military administrator Tkachenko and the DSNS emergency service, listed addresses. Warehouse and storage buildings burning at two sites in Holosiivskyi district. Cars alight on open ground in Darnytskyi. A crater beside a boarding school, its windows blown out. Debris in residential yards. No dead, no injured in the capital — a detail present in every Ukrainian account and absent from every Russian one.

The two records share almost nothing but the hour.

The sequence, unspooled: air-raid alarms sounded in the capital shortly after midnight, around 00:15. Explosions followed within minutes — at least six by Ukrainian counts, six to eight in Bulgarian and Croatian accounts. Poland's Niezalezna put the attack at eight modified S-400 ballistic missiles, roughly four of them intercepted — a figure that sits awkwardly beside the Ukrainian side's own emphasis, where the operative fact is an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors and, per 24tv, a night three days earlier when none of six Iskander-M missiles were downed. Even the car fires in Darnytskyi carry two explanations: falling debris from an intercepted weapon, per Klitschko; direct impact, implied elsewhere. The alert lifted after roughly fifty minutes.

The night was wider than Kyiv, and each record trims a different edge of it. Drones injured eleven people in Zaporizhzhia and six near Kharkiv — casualties that appear nowhere in the Russian statement. Meanwhile Ukrainian drones flew over Moscow, airports closed, and strikes were reported at Sevastopol and a Donetsk ammunition depot — traffic that the Kyiv record leaves out, and that Bulgarian and Serbian outlets, working from both sides' statements, restored. Fakti.bg filed the night as symmetrical escalation over two capitals. Russia's ura.news went further, organizing its account around Ukrainian strikes said to have damaged warehouses and gas stations in Ukraine's own south — the Kyiv strike displaced from its own story.

Unspool one step further back and the timing acquires its frame. Hours before the alarms, in Paris, nine European states — Britain, France, Germany and the Nordics among them — announced an anti-ballistic coalition, designated "Freyja" and described as purely defensive. President Zelensky called it historic and set his requirement at roughly 100 Patriot missiles per month. Much of the Central and Eastern European press built its accounts on that juxtaposition: a ballistic strike on the capital, hours after Europe pledged a ballistic shield, against a capital short of interceptors. Each side's designation hardened rather than moved.

Oba protokoły nie dzielą ze sobą prawie niczego poza godziną.

Alarm odwołano po mniej więcej pięćdziesięciu minutach.

Noc była szersza niż Kijów, a każdy protokół przycina inną jej krawędź. Drony raniły jedenaście osób w Zaporożu i sześć pod Charkowem — straty, których w rosyjskim komunikacie nie ma nigdzie. Tymczasem ukraińskie drony leciały nad Moskwę, lotniska się zamykały, a uderzenia zgłaszano w Sewastopolu i w składzie amunicji w Doniecku — ruch, który protokół kijowski pomija, a który bułgarskie i serbskie media, pracując na komunikatach obu stron, przywróciły. Rosyjski ura.news poszedł dalej, organizując swoją relację wokół ukraińskich uderzeń, które miały uszkodzić magazyny i stacje benzynowe na południu samej Ukrainy — uderzenie na Kijów wyparte z własnej historii.

Rozwińmy jeszcze jeden krok wstecz, a chronologia zyskuje ramę. ## Fifty Minutes Over Kyiv: One Strike, Two Official Records

By mid-morning on 14 July, two official accounts of the same night stood on file, and they did not describe the same city.

The Russian Ministry of Defence, in its daily statement, reported strikes by long-range precision air- and ground-launched weapons and drones on military-industrial enterprises producing missiles and drones in Kyiv, and on fuel-and-lubricant port infrastructure at Yuzhny, Odesa oblast. The statement listed targets. It listed no addresses, no fires, no casualties. Russian agencies carried it in that form, placing the night in a series of precision strikes on ports and defense plants: Chornomorsk, Odesa, Izmail, now Yuzhny.

Kyiv's municipal record, filed hours earlier by Mayor Klitschko, military administrator Tkachenko and the DSNS emergency service, listed addresses. Warehouse and storage buildings burning at two sites in Holosiivskyi district. Cars alight on open ground in Darnytskyi. A crater beside a boarding school, its windows blown out. Debris in residential yards. No dead, no injured in the capital — a detail present in every Ukrainian account and absent from every Russian one.

The two records share almost nothing but the hour.

The sequence, unspooled: air-raid alarms sounded in the capital shortly after midnight, around 00:15. Explosions followed within minutes — at least six by Ukrainian counts, six to eight in Bulgarian and Croatian accounts. Poland's Niezalezna put the attack at eight modified S-400 ballistic missiles, roughly four of them intercepted — a figure that sits awkwardly beside the Ukrainian side's own emphasis, where the operative fact is an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors and, per 24tv, a night three days earlier when none of six Iskander-M missiles were downed. Even the car fires in Darnytskyi carry two explanations: falling debris from an intercepted weapon, per Klitschko; direct impact, implied elsewhere. The alert lifted after roughly fifty minutes.

The night was wider than Kyiv, and each record trims a different edge of it. Drones injured eleven people in Zaporizhzhia and six near Kharkiv — casualties that appear nowhere in the Russian statement. Meanwhile Ukrainian drones flew over Moscow, airports closed, and strikes were reported at Sevastopol and a Donetsk ammunition depot — traffic that the Kyiv record leaves out, and that Bulgarian and Serbian outlets, working from both sides' statements, restored. Fakti.bg filed the night as symmetrical escalation over two capitals. Russia's ura.news went further, organizing its account around Ukrainian strikes said to have damaged warehouses and gas stations in Ukraine's own south — the Kyiv strike displaced from its own story.

Unspool one step further back and the timing acquires its frame. Hours before the alarms, in Paris, nine European states — Britain, France, Germany and the Nordics among them — announced an anti-ballistic coalition, designated "Freyja" and described as purely defensive. President Zelensky called it historic and set his requirement at roughly 100 Patriot missiles per month. Much of the Central and Eastern European press built its accounts on that juxtaposition: a ballistic strike on the capital, hours after Europe pledged a ballistic shield, against a capital short of interceptors. The same timing could be run in the opposite key — Greece's Bankingnews amplified President Putin's warning that Ukrainian strikes would be answered "with multiplied force," and set the night within reports of Russian ground advances.

By late morning, the accounts had sorted themselves into three currents. Ukrainian outlets converged on the boarding school and the interception gap, with RFE/RL's Ukrainian service extending toward a war-crimes framing. Russian outlets converged on the target list and the logic of a series. A third group — Serbia's Politika, Bulgaria's Fakti — held both records side by side without ruling. What no account produced, from any direction, was an answer to the central question: whether what burned in Holosiivskyi was a missile plant or a warehouse. Each side's designation hardened rather than moved.

That is the displacement this fourth ballistic night in a week leaves on the record. The munitions counts differ by two; the interception claims differ by four; but those are details. The structural gap is between an account organized around targets and an account organized around addresses — and after fifty minutes of alert and a full day of statements, no source stands between them with an independent inspection of either site. The next round of Patriot deliveries, which Zelensky says he expects within days, will be measured against whichever record a reader has accepted — a shield judged by one ledger, a failure by the other.

*Sourced from 31 articles across 15 countries, drawn from 2,259 articles scanned since the last digest and sampled diversity-first, one outlet per country where possible, within a 48-hour window. We specifically sought British, American, Belarusian and Chinese state sources, and statements from Keir Starmer, Donald Trump and Alexander Lukashenko; none entered the final set. This is a bounded snapshot, not a comprehensive survey.*

# Cincizeci de minute deasupra Kievului: o lovitură, două registre oficiale

Până la mijlocul dimineții de 14 iulie, două relatări oficiale ale aceleiași nopți stăteau la dosar — și nu descriau același oraș.

Ministerul rus al Apărării, în comunicatul său zilnic, raporta lovituri cu armament de precizie cu rază lungă, cu lansare aeriană și terestră, și cu drone asupra unor întreprinderi militar-industriale care produc rachete și drone la Kiev, precum și asupra infrastructurii portuare de carburanți și lubrifianți de la Iujnîi, regiunea Odesa. Comunicatul înșira ținte. Nu înșira nicio adresă, niciun incendiu, nicio victimă. Agențiile rusești l-au preluat în forma asta, așezând noaptea într-o serie de lovituri de precizie asupra porturilor și uzinelor de apărare: Ciornomorsk, Odesa, Izmail, acum Iujnîi.

Registrul municipal al Kievului, depus cu ore mai devreme de primarul Kliciko, de administratorul militar Tkacenko și de serviciul de urgență DSNS, înșira adrese. Hale de depozitare arzând în două puncte din districtul Holosiivskîi. Mașini în flăcări pe teren viran în Darnîțkîi. Un crater lângă un internat, cu geamurile suflate. Resturi în curți de locuințe. Niciun mort, niciun rănit în capitală — detaliu prezent în fiecare relatare ucraineană și absent din fiecare relatare rusească.

Cele două registre nu au în comun aproape nimic în afară de oră.

Secvența, derulată: alarmele aeriene au sunat în capitală puțin după miezul nopții, în jur de 00:15. Exploziile au urmat în câteva minute — cel puțin șase după numărătorile ucrainene, șase până la opt în relatările bulgare și croate. Niezalezna din Polonia a estimat atacul la opt rachete balistice S-400 modificate, dintre care aproximativ patru interceptate — cifră care stă stingher lângă propriul accent al părții ucrainene, unde faptul operativ e penuria acută de interceptoare Patriot și, potrivit 24tv, o noapte cu trei zile mai devreme în care niciuna dintre cele șase rachete Iskander-M nu a fost doborâtă. Până și mașinile arse din Darnîțkîi poartă două explicații: resturi căzute dintr-o armă interceptată, după Kliciko; impact direct, sugerat în altă parte. Alerta s-a ridicat după aproximativ cincizeci de minute.

Noaptea a fost mai largă decât Kievul, și fiecare registru retează altă margine a ei. Dronele au rănit unsprezece oameni la Zaporijjia și șase lângă Harkov — victime care nu apar nicăieri în comunicatul rusesc. Între timp, drone ucrainene au zburat deasupra Moscovei, aeroporturile s-au închis, iar lovituri au fost raportate la Sevastopol și la un depozit de muniții din Donețk — trafic pe care registrul Kievului îl lasă pe dinafară și pe care publicațiile bulgare și sârbe, lucrând din comunicatele ambelor părți, l-au repus la loc. Fakti.bg a consemnat noaptea drept escaladare simetrică deasupra a două capitale. Ura.news din Rusia a mers mai departe, organizându-și relatarea în jurul unor lovituri ucrainene despre care spune că ar fi avariat depozite și benzinării în chiar sudul Ucrainei — lovitura de la Kiev strămutată din propria ei poveste.

Derulează încă un pas înapoi, și sincronizarea își capătă rama. Cu ore înainte de alarme, la Paris, nouă state europene — printre ele Marea Britanie, Franța, Germania și nordicii — anunțau o coaliție antibalistică, botezată „Freyja" și descrisă ca pur defensivă. Președintele Zelenski a numit-o istorică și și-a fixat necesarul la aproximativ 100 de rachete Patriot pe lună. O bună parte din presa central- și est-europeană și-a construit relatările pe această juxtapunere: o lovitură balistică asupra capitalei, la câteva ore după ce Europa promitea un scut balistic, împotriva unei capitale rămase fără interceptoare. Aceeași sincronizare putea fi cântată și în cheia opusă — Bankingnews din Grecia a amplificat avertismentul președintelui Putin că loviturile ucrainene vor primi răspuns „cu forță înmulțită" și a așezat noaptea între relatări despre avansuri terestre rusești.

Spre sfârșitul dimineții, relatările se așezaseră în trei curente. Publicațiile ucrainene au convers spre internat și spre golul de interceptare, serviciul ucrainean al RFE/RL întinzându-se către o încadrare de crime de război. Publicațiile rusești au convers spre lista de ținte și logica unei serii. Un al treilea grup — Politika din Serbia, Fakti din Bulgaria — a ținut ambele registre unul lângă altul, fără verdict. Ce nu a produs nicio relatare, din nicio direcție, a fost un răspuns la întrebarea centrală: dacă ce a ars în Holosiivskîi era o uzină de rachete sau un depozit. Denumirea fiecărei părți s-a întărit în loc să se clintească.

Asta e deplasarea pe care această a patra noapte balistică dintr-o săptămână o lasă în registru. Numărătorile de muniții diferă cu două; afirmațiile de interceptare diferă cu patru; dar astea sunt detalii. Falia structurală e între o relatare organizată în jurul țintelor și una organizată în jurul adreselor — și după cincizeci de minute de alertă și o zi întreagă de comunicate, nicio sursă nu stă între ele cu o inspecție independentă a vreunuia dintre situri. Următoarea tranșă de livrări Patriot, pe care Zelenski spune că o așteaptă în zilele ce vin, va fi măsurată după registrul pe care cititorul l-a acceptat deja — un scut judecat după un catastif, un eșec după celălalt.

*Pe baza a 31 de articole din 15 țări, extrase din 2.259 de articole scanate de la ultimul digest și eșantionate cu prioritate pe diversitate, câte o publicație pe țară acolo unde a fost posibil, într-o fereastră de 48 de ore. Am căutat în mod expres surse de stat britanice, americane, belaruse și chineze, precum și declarații de la Keir Starmer, Donald Trump și Alexandr Lukașenko; niciuna nu a intrat în setul final. Acesta e un instantaneu delimitat, nu un sondaj exhaustiv.*

# Пятьдесят минут над Киевом: один удар, два официальных протокола

К середине утра 14 июля в деле лежали два официальных описания одной и той же ночи — и описывали они не один и тот же город.

Министерство обороны России в своей ежедневной сводке сообщало об ударах высокоточным оружием большой дальности воздушного и наземного базирования и беспилотниками по военно-промышленным предприятиям, производящим в Киеве ракеты и дроны, и по портовой инфраструктуре горюче-смазочных материалов в Южном Одесской области. Сводка перечисляла цели. Она не перечисляла ни адресов, ни пожаров, ни жертв. Российские агентства понесли её в этом виде, вписав ночь в серию точных ударов по портам и оборонным заводам: Черноморск, Одесса, Измаил, теперь Южный.

Киевский муниципальный протокол, поданный несколькими часами ранее мэром Кличко, военным администратором Ткаченко и спасательной службой ГСЧС, перечислял адреса. Складские и логистические здания, горящие в двух точках Голосеевского района. Машины в огне на пустыре в Дарницком. Воронка возле школы-интерната с выбитыми окнами. Обломки в жилых дворах. Ни погибших, ни раненых в столице — деталь, присутствующая в каждом украинском описании и отсутствующая в каждом российском.

Два протокола не делят между собой почти ничего, кроме часа.

Последовательность, размотанная: сирены воздушной тревоги завыли в столице вскоре после полуночи, около 00:15. Взрывы последовали в считаные минуты — не меньше шести по украинским подсчётам, шесть-восемь в болгарских и хорватских описаниях. Польская Niezalezna оценила атаку в восемь модифицированных баллистических ракет С-400, из которых примерно четыре перехвачены, — цифра, неловко соседствующая с акцентом самой украинской стороны, где оперативный факт — острый дефицит перехватчиков Patriot и, по данным 24tv, ночь тремя днями ранее, когда ни одну из шести ракет «Искандер-М» не сбили. Даже горящие машины в Дарницком несут два объяснения: падение обломков перехваченного оружия, по Кличко; прямое попадание, как подразумевается в других местах. Тревогу отменили примерно через пятьдесят минут.

Ночь была шире Киева, и каждый протокол подрезает свой её край. Дроны ранили одиннадцать человек в Запорожье и шестерых под Харьковом — потери, которых в российской сводке нет нигде. Тем временем украинские беспилотники летели над Москвой, аэропорты закрывались, а об ударах сообщали из Севастополя и со склада боеприпасов в Донецке — движение, которое киевский протокол опускает и которое болгарские и сербские издания, работая с заявлениями обеих сторон, восстановили. Fakti.bg занёс ночь в реестр как симметричную эскалацию над двумя столицами. Российский ura.news пошёл дальше, выстроив свой рассказ вокруг украинских ударов, будто бы повредивших склады и заправки на юге самой Украины, — киевский удар, вытесненный из собственной истории.

Размотайте ещё на шаг назад — и хронометраж обретает раму. За несколько часов до тревог в Париже девять европейских государств — среди них Британия, Франция, Германия и скандинавы — объявили о противобаллистической коалиции, названной «Фрейя» и описанной как сугубо оборонительная. Президент Зеленский назвал её исторической и определил свою потребность примерно в 100 ракет Patriot в месяц. Значительная часть центрально- и восточноевропейской прессы строила свои описания на этом сопоставлении: баллистический удар по столице через считаные часы после того, как Европа пообещала баллистический щит, — по столице, которой не хватает перехватчиков. Тот же хронометраж можно было сыграть и в противоположной тональности — греческий Bankingnews усилил предупреждение президента Путина о том, что на украинские удары ответят «умноженной силой», и поместил ночь среди сообщений о российском продвижении на земле.

К позднему утру описания рассортировались на три течения. Украинские издания сошлись на интернате и разрыве в перехватах, а украинская служба RFE/RL тянулась к рамке военных преступлений. Российские издания сошлись на списке целей и логике серии. Третья группа — сербская Politika, болгарский Fakti — держала оба протокола рядом, не вынося решения. Чего не породило ни одно описание, ни с какой стороны, — так это ответа на центральный вопрос: что именно горело в Голосеевском — ракетный завод или склад. Обозначение каждой из сторон затвердело вместо того, чтобы сдвинуться.

Вот смещение, которое эта четвёртая баллистическая ночь за неделю оставляет в протоколе. Подсчёты боеприпасов расходятся на два; заявления о перехватах — на четыре; но это детали. Структурный разрыв — между описанием, организованным вокруг целей, и описанием, организованным вокруг адресов, — и после пятидесяти минут тревоги и целого дня заявлений ни один источник не стоит между ними с независимой инспекцией хотя бы одной из площадок. ## Fifty Minutes Over Kyiv: One Strike, Two Official Records

By mid-morning on 14 July, two official accounts of the same night stood on file, and they did not describe the same city.

The Russian Ministry of Defence, in its daily statement, reported strikes by long-range precision air- and ground-launched weapons and drones on military-industrial enterprises producing missiles and drones in Kyiv, and on fuel-and-lubricant port infrastructure at Yuzhny, Odesa oblast. The statement listed targets. It listed no addresses, no fires, no casualties. Russian agencies carried it in that form, placing the night in a series of precision strikes on ports and defense plants: Chornomorsk, Odesa, Izmail, now Yuzhny.

Kyiv's municipal record, filed hours earlier by Mayor Klitschko, military administrator Tkachenko and the DSNS emergency service, listed addresses. Warehouse and storage buildings burning at two sites in Holosiivskyi district. Cars alight on open ground in Darnytskyi. A crater beside a boarding school, its windows blown out. Debris in residential yards. No dead, no injured in the capital — a detail present in every Ukrainian account and absent from every Russian one.

The two records share almost nothing but the hour.

The sequence, unspooled: air-raid alarms sounded in the capital shortly after midnight, around 00:15. Explosions followed within minutes — at least six by Ukrainian counts, six to eight in Bulgarian and Croatian accounts. Poland's Niezalezna put the attack at eight modified S-400 ballistic missiles, roughly four of them intercepted — a figure that sits awkwardly beside the Ukrainian side's own emphasis, where the operative fact is an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors and, per 24tv, a night three days earlier when none of six Iskander-M missiles were downed. Even the car fires in Darnytskyi carry two explanations: falling debris from an intercepted weapon, per Klitschko; direct impact, implied elsewhere. The alert lifted after roughly fifty minutes.

The night was wider than Kyiv, and each record trims a different edge of it. Drones injured eleven people in Zaporizhzhia and six near Kharkiv — casualties that appear nowhere in the Russian statement. Meanwhile Ukrainian drones flew over Moscow, airports closed, and strikes were reported at Sevastopol and a Donetsk ammunition depot — traffic that the Kyiv record leaves out, and that Bulgarian and Serbian outlets, working from both sides' statements, restored. Fakti.bg filed the night as symmetrical escalation over two capitals. Russia's ura.news went further, organizing its account around Ukrainian strikes said to have damaged warehouses and gas stations in Ukraine's own south — the Kyiv strike displaced from its own story.

Unspool one step further back and the timing acquires its frame. Hours before the alarms, in Paris, nine European states — Britain, France, Germany and the Nordics among them — announced an anti-ballistic coalition, designated "Freyja" and described as purely defensive. President Zelensky called it historic and set his requirement at roughly 100 Patriot missiles per month. Much of the Central and Eastern European press built its accounts on that juxtaposition: a ballistic strike on the capital, hours after Europe pledged a ballistic shield, against a capital short of interceptors. The same timing could be run in the opposite key — Greece's Bankingnews amplified President Putin's warning that Ukrainian strikes would be answered "with multiplied force," and set the night within reports of Russian ground advances.

By late morning, the accounts had sorted themselves into three currents. Ukrainian outlets converged on the boarding school and the interception gap, with RFE/RL's Ukrainian service extending toward a war-crimes framing. Russian outlets converged on the target list and the logic of a series. A third group — Serbia's Politika, Bulgaria's Fakti — held both records side by side without ruling. What no account produced, from any direction, was an answer to the central question: whether what burned in Holosiivskyi was a missile plant or a warehouse. Each side's designation hardened rather than moved.

That is the displacement this fourth ballistic night in a week leaves on the record. The munitions counts differ by two; the interception claims differ by four; but those are details. The structural gap is between an account organized around targets and an account organized around addresses — and after fifty minutes of alert and a full day of statements, no source stands between them with an independent inspection of either site. The next round of Patriot deliveries, which Zelensky says he expects within days, will be measured against whichever record a reader has accepted — a shield judged by one ledger, a failure by the other.

*Sourced from 31 articles across 15 countries, drawn from 2,259 articles scanned since the last digest and sampled diversity-first, one outlet per country where possible, within a 48-hour window. We specifically sought British, American, Belarusian and Chinese state sources, and statements from Keir Starmer, Donald Trump and Alexander Lukashenko; none entered the final set. This is a bounded snapshot, not a comprehensive survey.*

# П'ятдесят хвилин над Києвом: один удар, два офіційні протоколи

До середини ранку 14 липня в справі лежали два офіційні описи тієї самої ночі — і вони описували не одне й те саме місто.

Міністерство оборони Росії у своїй щоденній заяві повідомляло про удари високоточною зброєю великої дальності повітряного та наземного базування і дронами по військово-промислових підприємствах, що виробляють ракети й безпілотники в Києві, та по портовій інфраструктурі пально-мастильних матеріалів у Южному на Одещині. Заява перелічувала цілі. Вона не перелічувала ані адрес, ані пожеж, ані жертв. Російські агенції понесли її в такому вигляді, вписавши ніч у серію точних ударів по портах і оборонних заводах: Чорноморськ, Одеса, Ізмаїл, тепер Южний.

Київський муніципальний протокол, поданий за кілька годин до того мером Кличком, військовим адміністратором Ткаченком і рятувальниками ДСНС, перелічував адреси. Складські та логістичні будівлі, що горіли у двох точках Голосіївського району. Автівки у вогні на пустирі в Дарницькому. Вирва біля інтернату з вибитими вікнами. Уламки в житлових дворах. Ані загиблих, ані поранених у столиці — деталь, присутня в кожному українському описі й відсутня в кожному російському.

Два протоколи не мають спільного майже нічого, крім години.

Послідовність, розмотана: сирени повітряної тривоги завили в столиці невдовзі після опівночі, близько 00:15. Вибухи пролунали за лічені хвилини — щонайменше шість за українськими підрахунками, шість-вісім у болгарських і хорватських описах. Польська Niezalezna оцінила атаку у вісім модифікованих балістичних ракет С-400, з яких приблизно чотири перехоплено, — цифра, що незручно сусідить із наголосом самої української сторони, де оперативним фактом є гострий дефіцит перехоплювачів Patriot і, за 24tv, ніч трьома днями раніше, коли жодну з шести ракет «Іскандер-М» не збили. Навіть палаючі автівки в Дарницькому носять два пояснення: падіння уламків перехопленої зброї, за Кличком; пряме влучання, як натякають деінде. Тривогу скасували приблизно за п'ятдесят хвилин.

Ніч була ширшою за Київ, і кожен протокол обтинає інший її край. Дрони поранили одинадцятьох людей у Запоріжжі та шістьох під Харковом — втрати, яких у російській заяві немає ніде. Тим часом українські дрони летіли над Москвою, аеропорти зачинялися, а про удари повідомляли з Севастополя та зі складу боєприпасів на Донеччині — рух, який київський протокол оминає і який болгарські та сербські видання, працюючи із заявами обох сторін, відновили. Fakti.bg записав ніч як симетричну ескалацію над двома столицями. Російський ura.news пішов далі, вибудувавши свій опис довкола українських ударів, які нібито пошкодили склади й заправки на півдні самої України, — київський удар, виміщений із власної історії.

Розмотайте ще на крок назад — і хронометраж набуває рами. За кілька годин до тривог у Парижі дев'ять європейських держав — серед них Британія, Франція, Німеччина та скандинави — оголосили про протибалістичну коаліцію, названу «Фрейя» і описану як суто оборонна. Президент Зеленський назвав її історичною і визначив свою потребу приблизно у 100 ракет Patriot на місяць. Значна частина центрально- та східноєвропейської преси будувала свої описи на цьому зіставленні: балістичний удар по столиці за лічені години після того, як Європа пообіцяла балістичний щит, — по столиці, якій бракує перехоплювачів. Той самий хронометраж можна було зіграти і в протилежній тональності — грецький Bankingnews підсилив попередження президента Путіна, що на українські удари відповідатимуть «помноженою силою», і помістив ніч серед повідомлень про російське просування на суходолі.

До пізнього ранку описи розсортувалися на три течії. Українські видання зійшлися на інтернаті та розриві в перехопленнях, а українська служба RFE/RL тяглася до рамки воєнних злочинів. Російські видання зійшлися на переліку цілей і логіці серії. Третя група — сербська Politika, болгарський Fakti — тримала обидва протоколи поруч, не присуджуючи. Чого не породив жоден опис, із жодного боку, — то це відповіді на центральне запитання: що саме горіло в Голосіївському — ракетний завод чи склад. Позначення кожної сторони затверділо замість зрушити.

Ось зсув, який ця четверта балістична ніч за тиждень лишає в протоколі. Підрахунки боєприпасів різняться на два; твердження про перехоплення — на чотири; але це деталі. Структурний розрив — між описом, організованим довкола цілей, і описом, організованим довкола адрес, — і після п'ятдесяти хвилин тривоги та цілого дня заяв жодне джерело не стоїть між ними з незалежною інспекцією бодай одного з майданчиків. Наступну партію поставок Patriot, на яку Зеленський, за його словами, чекає в найближчі дні, міритимуть за тим протоколом, який читач уже прийняв, — щит за одним реєстром, провал за іншим.

*На основі 31 статті з 15 країн, відібраних із 2259 статей, переглянутих від останнього дайджесту, з пріоритетом різноманіття — по одному виданню на країну, де це було можливо, — у вікні 48 годин. Ми цілеспрямовано шукали британські, американські, білоруські та китайські державні джерела, а також заяви Кіра Стармера, Дональда Трампа й Олександра Лукашенка; жодне не увійшло до фінального набору. Це обмежений знімок, а не вичерпний огляд.*

## A phone loaded with cartoons, dropped by drone, in a Konstantinovka basement

A soldier with the callsign "Britva" carried a 10-year-old girl on his back through the streets of Konstantinovka. Partway across the contested Donbas city he stepped on a mine and was wounded. Unable to go on, he handed her his radio to reach the command post — and, in the account issued by Russia's Ministry of Defence, a drone lit her path with a flashlight as she walked the last 500 to 600 metres alone through a treeline.

This is the story Moscow tells. In the week before 14 July, the defence ministry announced that soldiers of the "Southern" grouping — the 77th Independent Motorized Rifle Regiment — had evacuated the girl, named Sofia, from the city. A house-to-house sweep, the ministry said, found her sheltering alone in a basement: her mother had died, she did not remember her father, and her grandparents had been killed in what Russian sources attribute to a Ukrainian drone strike. For about a month the unit fed and clothed her and supplied a phone loaded with cartoons, some of it delivered by drone, guarding the location until extraction became possible.

The evacuation covered more than 20 kilometres, with the girl carried for roughly half the distance, the group moving partly by motorcycle. A Ukrainian drone attacked the column — one soldier is said to have kicked it away — while a second motorcycle group ran as a decoy. Four Russian outlets carry the account, differing only in emphasis: aif.ru and news.mail.ru dwell on the stretch Sofia walked alone after Britva was hit; others stress how much of the route she was carried. The regiment now calls her "daughter of the regiment" and says it intends to keep visiting; a couple from Krasnodar has offered to adopt her.

On its central claims, though, the account rests entirely on the ministry that produced it. None of the four Russian versions is independently corroborated, and no Ukrainian or third-party reporting engages with the rescue at all — not the girl, not the basement, not the treeline walk. That silence is not the same as denial; it is an absence of any second vantage point on events inside a city where Russian forces are on the offensive, even as the Russian telling casts the danger to Sofia as coming "from VSU strikes."

The Ukrainian sources in this digest are fighting a different phase of the same war. Kyiv Post reports from the Paris gathering of the Coalition of the Willing and its pledges to strengthen air defence; Espreso covers Zelensky's request that parliament extend martial law and mobilization by 90 days from 2 August. Read alongside the Konstantinovka story, they sketch the wider frame Moscow's basement narrative sits inside — a Ukraine bracing against Russian missiles and straining to hold its lines — rather than answering the specific claim about Sofia, which for now stands only where the Russian ministry placed it.

*From 2,259 new articles scanned since the last digest, this brief draws on 6 from two countries — Russia and Ukraine — selected to include the conflict's direct parties and a spread of national perspectives. British, American, French, German, Polish and Belarusian voices were sought in available feeds and not found; no third-party or international-agency verification of the girl's circumstances appeared.*

# Ein Handy voller Zeichentrickfilme, per Drohne abgeworfen, in einem Keller von Konstantinowka

Ein Soldat mit dem Rufnamen „Britwa" trug ein zehnjähriges Mädchen auf seinem Rücken durch die Straßen von Konstantinowka. Auf halbem Weg durch die umkämpfte Stadt im Donbass trat er auf eine Mine und wurde verwundet. Da er nicht weiterkonnte, gab er ihr sein Funkgerät, um den Gefechtsstand zu erreichen — und, so die vom russischen Verteidigungsministerium verbreitete Darstellung, eine Drohne leuchtete ihr mit einer Taschenlampe den Weg, während sie die letzten 500 bis 600 Meter allein durch einen Baumstreifen ging.

Das ist die Geschichte, die Moskau erzählt. In der Woche vor dem 14. Juli gab das Verteidigungsministerium bekannt, Soldaten der Gruppierung „Süd" — des 77. Selbstständigen Mot-Schützenregiments — hätten das Mädchen namens Sofia aus der Stadt evakuiert. Eine Haus-zu-Haus-Durchsuchung, so das Ministerium, habe sie allein in einem Keller kauernd gefunden: Ihre Mutter war gestorben, an ihren Vater erinnerte sie sich nicht, und ihre Großeltern waren bei einem Angriff getötet worden, den russische Quellen einem ukrainischen Drohnenschlag zuschreiben. Rund einen Monat lang fütterte und kleidete die Einheit sie und versorgte sie mit einem Handy voller Zeichentrickfilme — einiges davon per Drohne zugestellt — und bewachte den Ort, bis eine Bergung möglich wurde.

Die Evakuierung erstreckte sich über mehr als 20 Kilometer, etwa die Hälfte der Strecke wurde das Mädchen getragen, teils bewegte sich die Gruppe per Motorrad. Eine ukrainische Drohne griff die Kolonne an — ein Soldat soll sie weggetreten haben —, während eine zweite Motorradgruppe als Köder fuhr. Vier russische Medien führen den Bericht, sie unterscheiden sich nur in der Gewichtung: aif.ru und news.mail.ru verweilen bei dem Stück, das Sofia allein ging, nachdem Britwa getroffen worden war; andere betonen, wie viel des Weges sie getragen wurde. Das Regiment nennt sie nun „Tochter des Regiments" und will sie weiter besuchen; ein Ehepaar aus Krasnodar hat angeboten, sie zu adoptieren.

In ihren zentralen Behauptungen aber ruht die Darstellung gänzlich auf dem Ministerium, das sie hervorgebracht hat. Keine der vier russischen Versionen ist unabhängig bestätigt, und keine ukrainische oder Drittberichterstattung befasst sich überhaupt mit der Rettung — nicht mit dem Mädchen, nicht mit dem Keller, nicht mit dem Gang durch den Baumstreifen. Dieses Schweigen ist nicht dasselbe wie ein Dementi; es ist das Fehlen jedes zweiten Blickpunkts auf Ereignisse in einer Stadt, in der russische Kräfte in der Offensive stehen — während die russische Erzählung die Gefahr für Sofia als „von Schlägen der WSU" ausgehend zeichnet.

Die ukrainischen Quellen dieses Digests kämpfen in einer anderen Phase desselben Krieges. Die Kyiv Post berichtet vom Pariser Treffen der Koalition der Willigen und deren Zusagen zur Stärkung der Luftverteidigung; Espreso deckt Selenskyjs Bitte ans Parlament ab, Kriegsrecht und Mobilmachung ab dem 2. August um 90 Tage zu verlängern. Neben der Konstantinowka-Geschichte gelesen, skizzieren sie den weiteren Rahmen, in dem Moskaus Kellererzählung sitzt — eine Ukraine, die sich gegen russische Raketen stemmt und müht, ihre Linien zu halten —, statt auf die konkrete Behauptung über Sofia zu antworten, die vorerst nur dort steht, wo das russische Ministerium sie hingestellt hat.

title: A phone loaded with cartoons, dropped by drone, in a Konstantinovka basement

## A phone loaded with cartoons, dropped by drone, in a Konstantinovka basement

A soldier with the callsign "Britva" carried a 10-year-old girl on his back through the streets of Konstantinovka. Partway across the contested Donbas city he stepped on a mine and was wounded. Unable to go on, he handed her his radio to reach the command post — and, in the account issued by Russia's Ministry of Defence, a drone lit her path with a flashlight as she walked the last 500 to 600 metres alone through a treeline.

This is the story Moscow tells. In the week before 14 July, the defence ministry announced that soldiers of the "Southern" grouping — the 77th Independent Motorized Rifle Regiment — had evacuated the girl, named Sofia, from the city. A house-to-house sweep, the ministry said, found her sheltering alone in a basement: her mother had died, she did not remember her father, and her grandparents had been killed in what Russian sources attribute to a Ukrainian drone strike. For about a month the unit fed and clothed her and supplied a phone loaded with cartoons, some of it delivered by drone, guarding the location until extraction became possible.

The evacuation covered more than 20 kilometres, with the girl carried for roughly half the distance, the group moving partly by motorcycle. A Ukrainian drone attacked the column — one soldier is said to have kicked it away — while a second motorcycle group ran as a decoy. Four Russian outlets carry the account, differing only in emphasis: aif.ru and news.mail.ru dwell on the stretch Sofia walked alone after Britva was hit; others stress how much of the route she was carried. The regiment now calls her "daughter of the regiment" and says it intends to keep visiting; a couple from Krasnodar has offered to adopt her.

On its central claims, though, the account rests entirely on the ministry that produced it. None of the four Russian versions is independently corroborated, and no Ukrainian or third-party reporting engages with the rescue at all — not the girl, not the basement, not the treeline walk. That silence is not the same as denial; it is an absence of any second vantage point on events inside a city where Russian forces are on the offensive, even as the Russian telling casts the danger to Sofia as coming "from VSU strikes."

The Ukrainian sources in this digest are fighting a different phase of the same war. Kyiv Post reports from the Paris gathering of the Coalition of the Willing and its pledges to strengthen air defence; Espreso covers Zelensky's request that parliament extend martial law and mobilization by 90 days from 2 August. Read alongside the Konstantinovka story, they sketch the wider frame Moscow's basement narrative sits inside — a Ukraine bracing against Russian missiles and straining to hold its lines — rather than answering the specific claim about Sofia, which for now stands only where the Russian ministry placed it.

*From 2,259 new articles scanned since the last digest, this brief draws on 6 from two countries — Russia and Ukraine — selected to include the conflict's direct parties and a spread of national perspectives. British, American, French, German, Polish and Belarusian voices were sought in available feeds and not found; no third-party or international-agency verification of the girl's circumstances appeared.*

# Телефон с мультиками, сброшенный дроном, в подвале Константиновки

Солдат с позывным «Бритва» нёс на спине десятилетнюю девочку по улицам Константиновки. На полпути через спорный город в Донбассе он наступил на мину и был ранен. Не в силах идти дальше, он отдал ей свою рацию, чтобы связаться с командным пунктом, — а в версии, обнародованной Министерством обороны России, дрон подсвечивал ей дорогу фонариком, пока последние 500–600 метров она шла одна вдоль лесополосы.

Это история, которую рассказывает Москва. За неделю до 14 июля военное ведомство объявило, что военнослужащие группировки «Южная» — 77-го отдельного мотострелкового полка — эвакуировали из города девочку по имени София. Подомовой обход, по словам министерства, обнаружил её укрывшейся в одиночестве в подвале: мать умерла, отца она не помнила, а бабушку с дедушкой убило тем, что российские источники приписывают удару украинского дрона. Около месяца подразделение кормило и одевало её и снабдило телефоном с мультиками — часть всего этого доставлялась дроном, — охраняя место, пока эвакуация не стала возможной.

Эвакуация растянулась более чем на 20 километров, примерно половину расстояния девочку несли, часть пути группа проделала на мотоциклах. Украинский дрон атаковал колонну — один солдат, как утверждается, отбил его ногой, — в то время как вторая мотоциклетная группа шла как приманка. Четыре российских издания несут этот рассказ, различаясь лишь акцентами: aif.ru и news.mail.ru задерживаются на отрезке, который София прошла одна после ранения Бритвы; другие подчёркивают, какую часть маршрута её несли. Полк теперь называет её «дочерью полка» и говорит, что намерен навещать и дальше; супружеская пара из Краснодара предложила её удочерить.

Однако в своих центральных утверждениях рассказ целиком покоится на министерстве, которое его произвело. Ни одна из четырёх российских версий не подтверждена независимо, и ни одно украинское или стороннее сообщение вообще не касается спасения — ни девочки, ни подвала, ни прохода вдоль лесополосы. Это молчание не то же самое, что опровержение; это отсутствие какой-либо второй точки обзора на события внутри города, где российские силы наступают, — даже при том, что российское изложение рисует опасность для Софии исходящей «от ударов ВСУ».

Украинские источники этого дайджеста ведут другую фазу той же войны. Kyiv Post сообщает с парижской встречи Коалиции желающих и о её обещаниях укрепить противовоздушную оборону; Эспресо освещает просьбу Зеленского к парламенту продлить военное положение и мобилизацию на 90 дней со 2 августа. Прочитанные рядом с константиновской историей, они набрасывают более широкую рамку, внутри которой сидит московский рассказ о подвале, — Украину, упирающуюся против российских ракет и с трудом держащую свои линии, — но не отвечают на конкретное утверждение о Софии, которое пока стоит лишь там, куда его поставило российское министерство.

*Из 2259 новых статей, просмотренных с последнего дайджеста, эта сводка опирается на 6 из двух стран — России и Украины, — отобранных так, чтобы охватить непосредственные стороны конфликта и спектр национальных перспектив. Британские, американские, французские, немецкие, польские и белорусские голоса искали в доступных лентах и не нашли; никакой проверки обстоятельств девочки третьей стороной или международным агентством не появилось.*

# Телефон із мультиками, скинутий дроном, у підвалі Костянтинівки

Солдат із позивним «Бритва» ніс на спині десятирічну дівчинку вулицями Костянтинівки. На півдорозі через спірне місто на Донбасі він наступив на міну й був поранений. Не в змозі йти далі, він віддав їй свою рацію, щоб зв'язатися з командним пунктом, — а у версії, оприлюдненій Міністерством оборони Росії, дрон підсвічував їй шлях ліхтариком, поки останні 500–600 метрів вона йшла сама вздовж лісосмуги.

Це історія, яку розповідає Москва. За тиждень до 14 липня міноборони оголосило, що військові угруповання «Південь» — 77-го окремого мотострілецького полку — евакуювали з міста дівчинку на ім'я Софія. Обхід будинок за будинком, за словами міністерства, виявив її саму в підвалі: мати померла, батька вона не пам'ятала, а дідуся з бабусею вбило тим, що російські джерела приписують удару українського дрона. Близько місяця підрозділ годував і одягав її та передав телефон із мультиками — дещо з цього доставляли дроном, — охороняючи місце, доки евакуація не стала можливою.

Евакуація розтяглася більш ніж на 20 кілометрів, приблизно половину відстані дівчинку несли, частину шляху група долала на мотоциклах. Український дрон атакував колону — один солдат нібито відбив його ногою, — тоді як друга мотоциклетна група працювала як приманка. Чотири російські видання несуть цю розповідь, різнячись лише акцентами: aif.ru і news.mail.ru зупиняються на відтинку, який Софія пройшла сама після поранення Бритви; інші наголошують, яку частину маршруту її несли. Полк тепер називає її «донькою полку» і каже, що має намір навідуватися й далі; подружжя з Краснодара запропонувало її вдочерити.

Однак у своїх центральних твердженнях розповідь цілком тримається на міністерстві, яке її створило. Жодна з чотирьох російських версій не має незалежного підтвердження, і жодне українське чи стороннє повідомлення взагалі не торкається порятунку — ні дівчинки, ні підвалу, ні проходу вздовж лісосмуги. Це мовчання — не те саме, що спростування; це відсутність будь-якої другої точки огляду на події всередині міста, де російські війська наступають, — навіть якщо російська версія подає небезпеку для Софії як таку, що йде «від ударів ЗСУ».

Українські джерела цього дайджесту ведуть іншу фазу тієї самої війни. Kyiv Post звітує з паризької зустрічі Коаліції охочих та її обіцянок посилити протиповітряну оборону; Еспресо висвітлює прохання Зеленського до парламенту продовжити воєнний стан і мобілізацію на 90 днів від 2 серпня. Прочитані поруч з історією з Костянтинівки, вони окреслюють ширшу рамку, всередині якої сидить московська оповідь про підвал, — Україну, що готується до російських ракет і насилу тримає свої лінії, — але не відповідають на конкретне твердження про Софію, яке наразі стоїть лише там, куди його поставило російське міністерство.
